current_description.description_long: The Atlantic’s January 2019 “Unthinkable” project surveyed Donald Trump’s first two years in office through a ranked list of 50 incidents. The page says the editors began with hundreds of moments and selected incidents they considered improbable, norm-bending and destructive; it describes the ranking as subjective and based on both outlandishness and importance. Its entries include Trump praising a congressman who had body-slammed a reporter, a secretary of state’s ouster by tweet, and the first president to complain about an election he had won. In a contemporaneous WBUR interview, Atlantic editor Adrienne LaFrance explained that the series examined norm-breaking in communication and treatment of institutions, from small daily acts to larger ones. These sources support a description of an editorial survey and its stated lens. They do not identify a particular constitutional reform or establish the abstract claim that a continuing pattern was “treated as structural.” The replacement title and text therefore describe the project itself and attribute its interpretation to its publishers.
current_description.description_medium: In January 2019, The Atlantic published an interactive catalog of 50 incidents from Donald Trump’s first two years as president. The magazine said its research team narrowed hundreds of candidates and ranked the selections subjectively for outlandishness and importance. The project documents the magazine’s framing of the presidency, not a specific institutional reform.
current_description.description_short: The Atlantic's 2019 project selected 50 incidents from Trump's first two years and framed them as improbable, norm-bending and destructive.

proposal.original_claim_summary: The entry says Trump suspended all federal research and educational funding to Harvard, Yale and Columbia together in August 2025 in retaliation for intellectual dissent.

identified_problems.explanation: Harvard and Columbia faced distinct funding actions on different dates and under separate administrative processes.
Major Columbia grant cancellations occurred March 7, 2025 and Harvard's initial $2.3 billion freeze was announced April 14, not in August.

The actions involved specified grants and contracts or future grant eligibility, not an established blanket suspension of every form of federal education and research funding to all three universities.
No comparable blanket Yale funding suspension matching the stored three-university claim was verified.

proposed_split_entries.proposed_title: Trump administration cancels about $400 million in Columbia grants and contracts
proposed_split_entries.proposed_synopsis: The administration canceled about $400 million in federal grants and contracts to Columbia University, citing what it described as failure to address antisemitic harassment. Columbia later negotiated with the government and regained most suspended funding under a July settlement.

proposed_split_entries.proposed_title: Administration freezes about $2.3 billion in Harvard grants and contracts after university rejects demands
proposed_split_entries.proposed_synopsis: After Harvard rejected a list of administration demands concerning campus governance, antisemitism, DEI and other policies, the administration froze about $2.2 billion in grants and $60 million in contract value.

claims.claim: About $400 million in Columbia grants and contracts were canceled in March 2025.
About $2.3 billion in Harvard grants and contract value were frozen in April 2025 after Harvard rejected administration demands.
All federal funding to Harvard, Yale and Columbia was suspended together in August 2025.

frozen_original.title: Trump Strips Federal Funding from Elite Universities
frozen_original.synopsis: In a retaliatory move against intellectual dissent, Trump ordered the suspension of all federal research and educational funding to Harvard, Yale, and Columbia universities in August 2025. He accused the institutions of being 'Marxist indoctrination camps' and harboring anti-American sentiment. The vindictive action threatened vital scientific research and academic freedom.

proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump allegedly held up a blank or nearly blank sheet at an October 15, 2020 rally and presented it as his healthcare plan.

identified_problems.explanation: Targeted searches of contemporaneous campaign reporting and fact-checks did not verify the described visual event.
The synopsis appears to combine documented criticism of Trump's unfulfilled healthcare-plan promises with an unverified blank-paper anecdote.

claims.claim: Trump displayed a blank sheet and represented it as his healthcare plan at an October 2020 campaign event.

frozen_original.title: Trump Holds Up Blank Paper Claiming It's His Healthcare Plan
frozen_original.synopsis: At a campaign rally, Trump held up what appeared to be a blank or nearly blank piece of paper, presenting it as his healthcare plan. After years of promising to replace the Affordable Care Act with a better plan, Trump had no substantive healthcare proposal to show. The image of a president holding up a blank page as his healthcare policy became a widely shared symbol of the lack of substance behind his policy rhetoric. Healthcare policy experts and journalists who examined Trump's actual healthcare proposals noted they contained no specific mechanisms for covering preexisting conditions or reducing costs. The moment crystallized years of criticism that Trump's healthcare promises were entirely performative.

identified_problems.explanation: No credible contemporaneous source was located establishing the described February 2025 federal investigation.

claims.claim: DOJ opened the described federal investigation into Fani Willis in February 2025.

frozen_original.title: Bondi DOJ Investigates Georgia DA Fani Willis for Trump RICO Prosecution
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump DOJ under Pam Bondi opened a federal investigation into Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis — who had indicted Trump and 18 co-defendants in a sweeping Georgia RICO case over efforts to overturn the 2020 election — examining her use of county funds and her personal relationship with a prosecutor on the case, the same relationship that had been litigated in Georgia state court and resolved without disqualification. The federal investigation was opened by an administration that had every interest in destroying the Georgia prosecution, using federal prosecutorial power to pile on existing state-level attacks on a prosecutor. Multiple federal judges and former prosecutors described the investigation as an unconstitutional interference with a state criminal proceeding and an abuse of executive power. The Georgia case, already burdened by state-level challenges and Trump's election to the presidency, was further disrupted.
